source.title: Adam Reduces a Unique Form of Sharpness: Theoretical Insights Near the Minimizer Manifold
source.authors: Xing-Hang Li; Hao-Dong Wen; Kaifeng Lyu

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no material truncation is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: Compares Adam and SGD on held-out loss in two controlled settings, using different tasks and measures from the benchmark comparisons in V4.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports theoretical results about implicit sharpness regularization and optimizer convergence. Those are not rows because they do not measure the versions’ named behavior. Figure 2’s plotted curves are described in text; exact values beyond the stated approximate recovery point are not reported in text.
record.test_reason: The study directly compares Adam and SGD on held-out loss in new synthetic neural-network settings. These results bear on V4's optimizer comparison, but do not establish its benchmark-specific or tuning-specific claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: Adam's distinct implicit sharpness bias helps sparse recovery in diagonal linear networks but worsens low-rank recovery in the tested matrix-factorization settings. The theoretical characterization assumes dynamics near a smooth minimizer manifold and the specified second-moment scaling; its simple diagonal-Hessian regularizer applies under label noise.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses controlled synthetic regression and matrix-factorization tasks with label noise, rather than the benchmark tasks and tuning comparisons described in V4. It reports standard Adam hyperparameters for the matrix-factorization experiment, but does not report a limited-tuning protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: Task and model structure change the relative test-loss outcome: Adam performs better in the sparse diagonal-net regression setting, while worse in deep matrix factorization at depths L = 2 and L = 5.

fits_no_version.finding: In matrix factorization, Adam reaches smaller tr(Diag(H)^(1/2)) but larger tr(H) and higher test loss than SGD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different Hessian-based sharpness measures can order optimizer solutions differently; reducing Adam's implicit sharpness measure need not improve generalization.

record.problems: The empirical comparisons are restricted to controlled synthetic tasks. Numerical test-loss values and uncertainty estimates for the plotted comparisons are not stated in the text. The paper notes that interpreting Adam’s diagonal-Hessian regularizer as a sparsity preference relies on the diagonal-net setting.
record.rows_left_out: None. Figure 2 also compares AdamE configurations, but those are optimizer variants used to examine the paper’s implicit-bias proposal, not the Adam-versus-SGD comparison named by V4.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting versus natural-label held-out accuracy; fresh training noise is a different manipulation.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Image-classification and language benchmarks; limited versus broader tuning; switching to SGD; decoupled weight decay; word-level language modeling.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and their dependence on training-set size, strength, or augmentation.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance as a predictor of generalization gaps, including comparisons with norm and margin measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: T3 is appropriate because the empirical method remains an Adam-versus-SGD held-out-performance comparison while the tasks change. Neither synthetic result establishes an effect of tuning breadth. Exact paired test-loss values and uncertainty estimates are unavailable in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization are not tested.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold test.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.

The study compares Adam with SGD on synthetic sparse regression and deep matrix factorization, not image-classification or language benchmarks; it does not compare limited hyperparameter tuning with broader tuning, or test switching optimizers or decoupled weight decay.
The study compares Hessian-derived sharpness quantities across optimizers, but does not test magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness as a predictor or rank it against norm- and margin-based measures.
